query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of aluminum into the refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a protective alumina (Al2O3) scale on its surface.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with minimal aluminum content, lacking a continuous protective oxide scale under oxidation.
generation.intervention: Alloying the base RHEA with a controlled addition (e.g., ~5 at.%) of aluminum via arc melting followed by homogenization.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1200°C in a pure oxygen atmosphere for 50 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense and adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The introduced aluminum preferentially oxidizes at high temperatures to form an Al2O3 scale. This scale is thermodynamically stable, exhibits low oxygen permeability, and acts as a diffusion barrier that slows further oxidation of the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Al-alloyed sample will show a significantly lower oxide weight gain and a more continuous, protective oxide scale, leading to improved oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy, which under identical conditions exhibits higher oxidation rates and less protective oxide scale formation.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvement is expected to be valid at 1200°C in a pure oxygen atmosphere for a duration of 50 hours; performance under other environmental conditions or temperatures may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., percentage reduction in mass gain) is uncertain and may depend on the final microstructural effects of Al addition and interactions with other alloying elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloy samples using identical synthesis routes: one set with a controlled addition (~5 at.%) of aluminum and one set without aluminum (control). Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation by exposing them in a furnace at 1200°C under a pure oxygen atmosphere for 50 hours. Monitor oxidation kinetics via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and characterize the oxide scales using SEM/EDS and XRD.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (mg/cm²) during oxidation
Surface oxide composition and continuity via SEM/EDS
Phase identification of the oxide scale via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in mass gain compared to the control or fail to form a dense, alumina-rich oxide layer after 50 hours at 1200°C in pure oxygen, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
